title: Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179)
hookLine: abbess, composer, healer and visionary, named a Doctor of the Church

cards: A sung play. On stage, a soul, a chorus of virtues, and the devil. Everyone sings except the devil.
He only shouts. The woman who wrote it also wrote songs for her sisters to sing in chapel, books on plants and healing, and letters that told popes and emperors exactly what she thought.
She led a community of nuns by the river Rhine, and she said she saw visions. Her name was Hildegard.

teach.h: WRITE WHAT YOU SEE AND HEAR.
teach.b: Hildegard was a Benedictine nun, and later an abbess. She says she saw visions from childhood and kept quiet about them for a long time.
Then, at the opening of her book Scivias, she writes that a fiery light poured into her mind, and a voice told her to write what she saw and heard.
Doubt held her back, she says, until illness pressed her, and she began, with help from a monk and one of her sisters. The title means, roughly, know the ways.

teach.h: CHANTS AND A PLAY OF VIRTUES.
teach.b: She wrote music too: long, soaring chants for her community to sing, and that play of the virtues, where the soul is pulled between them and the devil who cannot sing.
One word runs through her writing: viriditas, greenness. For her it meant the life God pours into everything: sap in a branch, health in a body, freshness in a soul. A soul could dry up.
It could also turn green again. It's the psalm's picture, in the Douay-Rheims: a person who is "like a tree which is planted near the running waters".
She wrote about herbs and healing, preached, and wrote to the powerful without softening her words.
Centuries after her death, Pope Benedict the Sixteenth named her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Church.
Visionary, composer, healer, abbess, and in all of it one conviction: life is given, and a dried-up soul can turn green again.

how: Catholics honor Saint Hildegard as a Doctor of the Church; her chants are sung by choirs and recorded, her writings are read on retreat, and the community at Eibingen keeps her memory by the Rhine.

an abbess who wrote of the green life God gives
a nun who copied Bibles in a riverside abbey

a tree near the running waters

s: Hildegard wrote only about her visions
she wrote chants, a sung play, books on plants and healing, and letters to the powerful.
for her, the life God pours into branch, body and soul.
Hildegard wrote down her visions the moment she had them

games.q: you've seen visions since childhood and kept them to yourself. now a voice says: write what you see and hear. what do you do?
o: keep it to yourself for good.
hold back, then begin to write, with help from a monk and a sister.
announce it to the whole town at once.
games.why: Hildegard says doubt held her back until illness pressed her; then she began Scivias, with a monk and one of her sisters helping.

practice: Notice something green: a plant on the sill, a tree outside, moss on a wall, or one you remember. Look at it the way Hildegard might, as life given, not made by you, and breathe with it.
If you pray, hold the psalm's picture, a tree planted near the running waters.

wordCard.voice: Hildegard. A Benedictine abbess, visionary, composer and healer, who spoke of viriditas, the green life God gives, and was named a Doctor of the Church. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: greenness. Hildegard's word for the life God gives to creation and to the soul.

carryVoice: Your line: the green life. The next story is a harder one to hear. Until tomorrow.
